content.title: response to Reviewer sHTK
content.comment:
Q: “Unfair comparison. The average attack budgets, i.e., the average malicious clients in each round, of different methods (tradition, CL, RCL) are different. Therefore, the comparison is unfair. Similarly, the comparison among different CLP detection thresholds (Figure 5) is unfair.”

A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding again. First, for CL and tradition, the average attack budget of CL is smaller than that of the tradition.  This exactly validates our claim in the paper that via leveraging the critical learning periods that detected from the deep neural networks, the attack impact can be improved by the attack using an adaptive attack budget rather than using a fixed attack budget in each round, even when the average attack budget is smaller, i.e., by adaptively attack the number of clients, the attack impact is improved by attacking a smaller number of clients on average.  

Second, the average attack budget of RCL is larger than that of CL and Tradition.  This also exactly validates our claim in the paper about the “Importance of properly leveraging CLP” in Section 3.2.2 on page 6.  In short, under RCL, a larger number of clients are attacked in each round on average, however, RCL leverages the CLP in a wrong way, which actually does not bring any benefits on the attack impact compared to Tradition (see Figure 2).  This supports the design of “CL” (more precisely the A-CLP approach in this paper, see Algorithm 1) that more clients should be attacked during the CLP.  

More discussions can be found in the paper, in particular Section 3.2.2 on page 6 and the “Takeaway 1”.  To this end, there is not the fairness or unfairness issue, but statements and experimental designs that strongly support our claims in the paper.

content.title: response to Reviewer sHTK
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the review.  

Q: “The setting is unrealistic…”
A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding.  First, as we discussed in Section 2 “Threat model”.  The adversary has control over M out of N total clients in the system, with M/N<50%.  In our experiments, we set N=128 and M=32, which satisfies this condition.  In other words, for both A-CLP and A, the adversary always controls M (not m) clients in each round, hence there is no unfairness issue. 

Second, as motivated by practice that only a small subset of clients participates in each training round in federated learning systems (Also the settings in many state-of-the-art works), in each round, the server randomly selects n clients for training (Note it is n not N, and in our experiments, we set n=16), see Section 2 “Federated learning” for details.  In traditional attacks A, the adversary often consistently involves m clients throughout the whole training process (Note that it is m, not M, and in our experiments, we set m=4), while in our A-CLP, the adversary leverages the information of critical learning periods to adaptively determine the number of malicious clients to be invoked, e.g., either m/2 or 2m.  

Finally, in Appendix E, we provide a theoretical study on the “Feasibility guarantee for the A-CLP framework” to answer the question of how many clients in total (denoted as M) should the adversary A control so that our A-CLP framework is feasible.  Our theoretical analysis and the corresponding empirical study in Appendix E support that our experimental settings, i.e., N=128, M=32 (and n=16, m=4) is feasible.  

Q: “The claim that sharing more malicious gradients in each round causes attacks to be more detectable is not convincing. In fact, when the number of malicious gradients is more than half of the total number of gradients, no defenses can successfully detect malicious gradients [5]. Please further illustrate it or provide empirical evidence.”

A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding as well.  Your statement that “when the number of malicious gradients is more than half of the total number of gradients, no defenses can successfully detect malicious gradients” is correct, which is exactly what we stated in Section 2 “Threat Model-Adversary’s capability” that M/N <50%.  This is exactly the setting we consider in our paper, and in our experiments, we set N=128 and M=32, which satisfies this condition.  Following the response above, in practice, the server randomly selects n out N clients for training in each round, where we set n=16 in our experiments.  Among these clients including m=4 malicious clients that are invoked by the adversary.  All our discussions in this paper satisfy that M/N<50%.  

Q: “It is impossible that there are 4 malicious clients in each round since the server randomly selects clients in each round!! Similarly, increasing the number of malicious gradients in critical learning periods is impossible.”

A: Thank you for this comment.  in Appendix E, we provide a theoretical study on the “Feasibility guarantee for the A-CLP framework” to answer the question of how many clients in total (denoted as M) should the adversary A control so that our A-CLP framework is feasible.  Our theoretical analysis and the corresponding empirical study in Appendix E support that our experimental settings, i.e., N=128, M=32 (and n=16, m=4) is feasible.

Q: “However, the comparison between A and A-CLP is unfair. Currently the authors assume that for A, the adversary invokes m malicious clients in each round while in A-CLP, the adversary invokes either m/2 or 2m malicious clients. This does not make sense because if the adversary can invoke 2m clients whenever it wants, that means it controls 2m clients in every round so a fair comparison with A needs to have 2m malicious clients in every round.”

A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding on the paper as well as on the threat model.  

First, as we discussed in Section 2 “Threat model”.  The adversary has control over M out of N total clients in the system, with M/N<50%.  In our experiments, we set N=128 and M=32, which satisfies this condition.  In other words, for both A-CLP and A, the adversary always controls M (not m) clients in each round, hence there is no unfairness issue. 

Second, as motivated by practice that only a small subset of clients participates in each training round in federated learning systems (Also the settings in many state-of-the-art works), in each round, the server randomly selects n clients for training (Note it is n not N, and in our experiments, we set n=16), see Section 2 “Federated learning” for details.  In traditional attacks A, the adversary often consistently involves m clients throughout the whole training process (Note that it is m, not M, and in our experiments, we set m=4), while in our A-CLP, the adversary leverages the information of critical learning periods to adaptively determine the number of malicious clients to be invoked, e.g., either m/2 or 2m.  

Finally, in Appendix E, we provide a theoretical study on the “Feasibility guarantee for the A-CLP framework” to answer the question of how many clients in total (denoted as M) should the adversary A control so that our A-CLP framework is feasible.  Our theoretical analysis and the corresponding empirical study in Appendix E support that our experimental settings, i.e., N=128, M=32 (and n=16, m=4) is feasible.

content.title: response to Reviewer 137d
content.comment:
Q: “It’s unclear why FGN is advantageous to choose the critical learning period and the threshold for FGN is handcrafted to determine, is that correct? So the adaptive attack budget still needs to try different threshold hyper-parameter for a better result.” 

A: As motivated in the paper, to leverage the CLP into the model poisoning attack, the first task to how to efficiently detect CLP in the federated training.  To our best knowledge, Gang et al. 2022 is the first work to provide a comprehensive experimental study on detecting CLP in federated setting.  However, their proposed method FedFIM is computationally expensive and hardly to be leveraged into model poisoning attack algorithms.  To this end, we proposed a lightweight FGN metric, which not only can detect the CLP almost as the same as those detected by FedFIM (See Figure 3), but is also more computationally efficient (see Figure 11).  With this FGN metric, we propose a threshold type rule to determine whether a learning phase is in the CLP or not (see Section 3.1).  For any given threshold $\delta$, we can detect the CLP and leverage it to adaptive model poisoning attack to FL.  Hence, the adaptive attack budget is independent of the $\delta$, i.e., no matter what the $\delta$ is, we can always design an adaptive attack budget policy.  However, different values of the $\delta$ may have an impact on the improvement of such an adaptive attack budget based model poisoning attack compared to traditional method.  Hence, we conducted an ablation study on the impact of $\delta$ as shown in Figure 5.  In practice, we can set $\delta$ to be a small value, such as $\delta=0.01$.  

Q: “Is this method still favorable in other scenarios like NLP. “

A: Yes.  In Section 3.2.1. “Dataset", we discussed two classes of datasets.  One is for image classification tasks including CIFAR-10, MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.  The other is for natural language processing tasks on next-character prediction using the Shakespeare dataset.  The corresponding results are provided in Appendix C.8. 

Q: “Some typos in Figures like Figure5 Final Accuracy rather than Accutacy. “

A: Thank you for pointing this out.  We will fix them and update the corresponding figures in the revised version.

content.title: response to Reviewer xBrr
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed review.  

Q: “Though CLP achieves better attack impact compared to traditional attacks with similar or lower attack budget on average, this method requires more clients to perturb. It is not clear how the performance difference is when the traditional attack methods utilize all these clients”

A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding.  You are right that our CLP aware attack actually has a similar or lower attack budget on average than traditional approaches as shown in Figure 5.  In particular, in each round, there are 4 malicious clients in the traditional approach, while there are 8 malicious clients during the CLP and 2 malicious clients after the CLP in our CLP aware attack.  Hence the number of perturbed clients after the CLP is smaller in our CLP aware attack than that of the traditional approach.  In total, the number of perturbed clients is also smaller.  Furthermore, we conducted an ablation study to investigate the impact of the number of malicious clients in Section 3.2.3 as shown in Figure 6.

Q: “ In the paragraph on improved resilience against defenses, the paper simply claims that a lower average budget implies better robustness. With the varying number of malicious clients, I don't think this is obvious, and I suggest the authors provide a quantitative comparison.”

A: Thank you for your suggestion.  Our claim is under the assumption that the total number of malicious clients is under less than 50% (see Section 2).  Figure 6 also studies the impact of the number of participated malicious client.  We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and we will add more direct experiments to make the comparison in the revised version.  

Q: “Lack of evaluation like robustness against defense against SimAttack-CLP”

A: We are afraid that there is a misunderstanding here as well.  We have evaluated the robustness against defense of SimAttack-CLP in Section 4 as shown in Figure 8.  

Q: “ If the paper claims SimAttack-CLP reduces the computational complexity, it is better to report the time difference.” 

A: We mainly discussed the complexity of the design of SimAttack-CLP from the optimization perspective, as discussed in “Intuition” and “the design of SimAttack-CLP”.  You have given a good suggestion.  We will also support this theoretical insight with some experimental results in the revised version.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an attack by adaptively adjusting the number of malicious clients per communication. Inspired by Critical Learning Periods (CLP), they observe that when the training loss difference between two communication rounds is high (usually at the beginning of the training), the learning procedure is easier to perturb. With distributing a higher portion of the attack budget on these communication rounds, it is easier to achieve high attack impact compared to traditional fixed number of malicious clients throughout the whole training procedure. For any given attacking algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, they could apply this adaptive malicious client mechanism $\mathcal{A}$-CLP. They also propose a simplified version of attack algorithm $SimAttack$-CLP which avoids heavy computation burden of most traditional attack methods when they compute malicious gradients.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
•	The proposed method is a simple and effective add-on for most of the current attack methods.
•	The paper is well organized and easy to follow.
•	The paper puts in a good effort on empirical evaluations.

Weaknesses:
•	[Major] Though CLP achieves better attack impact compared to traditional attacks with similar or lower attack budget on average, this method requires more clients to perturb. It is not clear how the performance difference is when the traditional attack methods utilize all these clients.
•	[Major] In the paragraph on improved resilience against defenses, the paper simply claims that a lower average budget implies better robustness. With the varying number of malicious clients, I don't think this is obvious, and I suggest the authors provide a quantitative comparison. 
•	[Major] Lack of evaluation like robustness against defense against $SimAttack$-CLP.
•	[Minor] If the paper claims $SimAttack$-CLP reduces the computational complexity, it is better to report the time difference.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper writing is clear and easy to follow.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The major concern is that if the adversary controls $m$ clients, and only uses all the clients at the beginning but not later in the training, it is still a tradeoff between attack impact and resilience against defenses. 

The comparison using average attack budget to claim better robustness against defense lacks experimental support.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength：
This paper provides a novel CLP plugin to solve the tradeoff between attack impact and attack budget, SimAttack-CLP to avoid a complex optimization. 
Sufficient experiments to prove the efficiency and effectiveness of A-CLP, e.g., the improved attack impact, and resilience against defenses.
The results seem to be reproducible and code was provided.
The paper is written clearly and easy to understand， especially the takeaway for the summary of the previous content.

Weakness: 
It’s unclear why FGN is advantageous to choose the critical learning period and the threshold for FGN is handcrafted to determine, is that correct? So the adaptive attack budget still needs to try different threshold hyper-parameter for a better result. 
More detailed related work about CLP is needed to understand the background.
More ablation studies about the different measurements in SimAttack-CLP are required.
Is this method still favorable in other scenarios like NLP. 
Some typos in Figures like Figure5 Final Accuracy rather than Accutacy.
A weakness analysis of this work is preferred.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a novel augmentation of model poisoning attacks based on the detection of critical learning periods called CLP. CLP is motivated by a recent finding that small gradient errors have an irrecoverable impact on model accuracy in critical learning periods. CLP uses federated gradient norms to detect critical learning periods in the FL training process. CLP increases the number of malicious gradients in detected critical learning periods. Experimental results verify the efficacy of CLP augmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

* The idea to utilize critical learning periods to maximize the attack impact is interesting.

Weaknesses:

* The setting is unrealistic. In the abstract, the authors assume that
  
  > Existing attacks ... share a fixed number of malicious gradients with the central server in each training round, ...
  
  In each training round, the FL server randomly samples a subset of clients to participate in training [1, 2]. Besides, the clients controlled by the adversary are fixed [3, 4]. Therefore, the number of malicious gradients is random rather than fixed.

* Unconvincing motivation. In the introduction, the authors write
  
  > However, such attack impact improvements are at the cost of sharing more malicious gradients in each round, which in turn causes these poisoning attacks to be more detectable by existing defenses.
  
  The claim that sharing more malicious gradients in each round causes attacks to be more detectable is not convincing. In fact, when the number of malicious gradients is more than half of the total number of gradients, no defenses can successfully detect malicious gradients [5]. Please further illustrate it or provide empirical evidence.

* Improper experimental settings. In section 3, the authors write
  
  > By default, we consider a total number of N = 128 clients in our experiments and the adversary controls M = 32 clients. In each round, the FL central server randomly selects n = 16 clients to participate in the global model update, in which m = 4 are malicious clients.
  
  It is impossible that there are 4 malicious clients in each round since the server *randomly* selects clients in each round!! Similarly, increasing the number of malicious gradients in critical learning periods is impossible.

* Unfair comparison. The average attack budgets, i.e., the average malicious clients in each round, of different methods (tradition, CL, RCL) are different. Therefore, the comparison is unfair. Similarly, the comparison among different CLP detection thresholds (Figure 5) is unfair. 

[1] McMahan, Brendan, et al. "Communication-efficient learning of deep networks from decentralized data." *Artificial intelligence and statistics*. PMLR, 2017.

[2] Li, Tian, et al. "Federated optimization in heterogeneous networks." *Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems* 2 (2020): 429-450.

[3] Blanchard, Peva, et al. "Machine learning with adversaries: Byzantine tolerant gradient descent." *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 30 (2017).

[4] Guerraoui, Rachid, and Sébastien Rouault. "The hidden vulnerability of distributed learning in byzantium." *International Conference on Machine Learning*. PMLR, 2018.

[5] Shejwalkar, Virat, and Amir Houmansadr. "Manipulating the byzantine: Optimizing model poisoning attacks and defenses for federated learning." *NDSS*. 2021.

Overall, I think the paper is below the bar of ICLR.

content.title: Critical Learning Periods Augmented Model Poisoning Attacks to Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning
content.abstract: Existing attacks in federated learning (FL) control a set of malicious clients and share a fixed number of malicious gradients with the central server in each training round, to achieve a desired tradeoff between attack impact and resilience against defenses.  In this paper, we show that such a tradeoff is not fundamental and an adaptive attack budget not only improves the impact of attack $\mathcal{A}$ but makes it more resilient to defenses.  Inspired by recent findings on critical learning periods (CLP), where small gradient errors have irrecoverable impact on model accuracy, we advocate CLP augmented model poisoning attacks $\mathcal{A}$-CLP, which merely augment attack $\mathcal{A}$ with an adaptive attack budget scheme. $\mathcal{A}$-CLP inspects the changes in federated gradient norms to identify CLP and adaptively adjusts the number of malicious clients that share their malicious gradients with the central server in each round, leading to dramatically improved attack impact compared to $\mathcal{A}$ itself by up to 6.85$\times$, with a smaller attack budget and hence improved resilience of $\mathcal{A}$ by up to 2$\times$.  Based on understandings on $\mathcal{A}$-CLP, we further relax the inner attack subroutine $\mathcal{A}$ in $\mathcal{A}$-CLP, and propose SimAttack-CLP, a lightweight CLP augmented similarity-based attack, which is more flexible and impactful.
